items.title: Google DeepMind releases Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash with enhanced generative video controls including scene extension, frame interpolation, and 4K upscaling [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash lets you build with more control
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has launched Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, an update to its generative video model that offers developers improved control over video creation. The new features include the ability to extend scenes up to 40 seconds with better visual consistency, specify start and end frames for smooth transitions, and upscale output to 4K resolution. Developers can access the model through Google AI Studio or the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

The update also introduces faster prototyping with 360p previews to reduce costs during iteration. Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash supports more complex video storytelling by analyzing up to 10 seconds of prior context, enabling longer and more coherent video sequences. These enhancements aim to make generative video production more practical and polished for professional use in creative and media editing applications.

items.title: Open source maintainer warns against AI-generated pull requests flooding projects to boost contributor profiles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Please stop flooding our projects with AI slop to furnish your CV
items.summary:
An open source maintainer has raised concerns about a recent surge in AI-generated contributions to projects, which appear aimed more at enhancing contributors' GitHub profiles than improving the projects themselves. These contributions include pull requests fixing minor issues like spelling and grammar, as well as AI-generated security vulnerability reports with proposed fixes.

The maintainer noted that while some contributions may come from genuine interest, many seem to be attempts to game GitHub's contribution metrics using AI tools like Claude. This trend has led to increased selectivity in accepting contributions and issuing CVE notices, emphasizing that meaningful improvements and genuine engagement, rather than quantity of AI-generated contributions, should be the focus in open source collaboration.

items.title: Developer reports breakthrough with small AI models like gpt-5.6-luna, highlighting low cost and high speed for business and consumer applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Small Models Have Arrived
items.summary:
A developer has been testing the small AI model gpt-5.6-luna and found it to be surprisingly capable, fast, and cost-effective, achieving around 100 transactions per second with API costs in the tens of cents. This contrasts with previous models that were too expensive for consumer apps, suggesting small models could enable new AI-powered products with manageable inference costs.

The developer discusses the challenges of integrating AI into consumer products due to high token costs and notes that small models like luna reduce these costs significantly, making personalized AI services more feasible. They also highlight the demand in business settings for "fast/cheap/good-enough" AI models to handle routine tasks efficiently, alongside the continued need for advanced models for complex problem-solving.

The article emphasizes the potential growth of small AI models in both consumer and business markets, while acknowledging the technical work needed to ensure safety and usability. The author invites others experimenting with small models to connect and collaborate.

items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 3.5 Transcribe for precise, intelligent real-time speech-to-text transcription with multi-language and multi-speaker support [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Intelligent transcription with Gemini 3.5 Transcribe
items.summary:
Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, a speech-to-text model designed for accurate, real-time transcription that handles background noise, jargon, and disfluencies. The model supports over 85 languages, multi-speaker identification, and custom vocabulary, improving transcription quality and latency compared to previous versions.

Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is available via two APIs for real-time streaming and pre-recorded audio processing, enabling developers to build voice agents, captioning tools, and analytics pipelines. It integrates with Google products like the Gemini app, Gboard, and Google AI Studio, offering smart transcription features such as filler word removal, auto-formatting, and function calling for complex tasks.

The model achieves low word error rates and supports seamless language switching and speaker attribution, representing a significant advancement in speech recognition technology for both consumer and enterprise applications.

items.title: Researchers measure invocation-level reliability of tool-using AI agents, revealing early errors cause significant downstream failures and proposing a new scoring method to better estimate error severity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents
items.summary:
Researchers studied how AI agents using tools fail by either selecting the wrong tool or forming incorrect arguments, which can silently corrupt subsequent steps. They measured correct-invocation rates across five open-weight models on multi-step tasks and found that by the sixth step, about 70% of the model's capability is lost due to earlier mistakes. The study highlights that traditional exact-match scoring fixes error severity and recovery parameters, making them hard to estimate accurately because the model cannot access certain post-divergence information.

The team identified that after divergence from the correct path, the gold standard values are generated by tool constants unknown to the model, causing structural unobservability of recovery. They introduced a conditional-on-state scoring method applied retrospectively to cached completions, which allows for more accurate interior estimates of error severity without additional computational cost. This approach unpins severity estimates from fixed boundaries, improving reliability measurement for tool-using agents.

items.title: Researchers present CorporateBench, a large-scale multi-task Q&A benchmark with over 230,000 documents to evaluate LLMs on enterprise communication reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated benchmark designed to test large language models (LLMs) on complex questions derived from enterprise-scale document collections. CB includes evaluation corpora from four synthetic firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees, with datasets exceeding 230,000 documents sampled from temporally evolving knowledge bases to ensure logical consistency across documents.

The benchmark assesses LLMs on information extraction and knowledge base querying tasks, revealing that model performance declines as input size approaches realistic corporate scales. CorporateBench aims to fill a gap in existing evaluation tools by providing a metric tailored to reasoning over corporate communication networks, which are typically difficult to access due to privacy concerns.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.27391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

items.originalTitle: FIRSTPASS: A Multi-Domain, Multi-Round Peer Review Dataset Grounded in Real Editorial Outcomes
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced FIRSTPASS, the first extensive peer review dataset covering multiple scientific domains, sourced from Nature Communications' transparent peer review process starting November 2022. The dataset includes 3,668 records across biology, chemistry, neuroscience, physics, and earth science, capturing initial referee reports, author responses, and updated reviewer assessments, with outcome labels based on editorial decisions.

FIRSTPASS offers detailed, multi-round peer review dialogues averaging 2,155 words per expert review, significantly denser than typical conference reviews. The dataset, along with parsing pipelines and evaluation scripts, is publicly released to support reproducible benchmarking of AI systems' scientific judgment across diverse disciplines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific peer review datasets have trained AI systems exclusively on Computer Science and Machine Learning venues, producing models that critique ablation studies yet have never seen a biology reviewer demand contamination controls or a chemist question Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectral assignments. We introduce FIRSTPASS, the first large-scale peer review dataset built on complete multi-round editorial dialogues from a multidisciplinary high-impact journal. Curated from Nature Communications mandatory transparent peer review (instituted November 2022), FIRSTPASS comprises 3,668 records spanning five scientific domains (biology, chemistry, neuroscience, physics, and earth science), capturing the full iterative structure of scientific validation: initial referee reports, author point-by-point responses, and updated reviewer assessments. Each record carries an outcome label derived directly from editorial decisions (STANDARD for two-round review; EXTENDED for three or more rounds), providing ground truth absent in all prior corpora. An automated audit confirms 100% content integrity. Expert reviews average 2,155 words, substantially denser than conference venue reviews. All data, parsing pipelines, and evaluation scripts are released to enable reproducible benchmarking of AI scientific judgment across disciplines.

items.title: Researchers formalize and measure the 'jump' in large language models, defining it as a deviation from canonical completions and testing it on multiple models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When the Canonical Completion Is Wrong: Formalizing and Measuring the Jump in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed a formal framework to define and measure the 'jump'—an abductive leap from evidence to new axioms—in large language models (LLMs). They define a jump instance as a finite extension problem with a machine-verified certificate that a correct completion exists, is unique up to renaming, and differs from the canonical completion, which models produce by default without constraints. The study tested nine certified jump instances across four advanced LLMs, finding that models consistently abandon the canonical default when forced, indicating that the inability to perform jumps is not due to reverting to default completions but may lie in generating constraints or frameworks. The research provides a structured approach to evaluating LLM reasoning capabilities beyond default completions and offers code for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can perform the abductive leap from evidence to a new system of axioms, commonly referred to as a jump, has recently attracted considerable debate. A prominent position holds that LLMs are structurally incapable of such jumps, while recent studies challenge both its mechanism and its evidence. However, the debate remains difficult to settle, since the field still lacks a formal definition of the jump and a measure to test either side. In this paper, we develop a formal account of the jump in four steps and measure the second. The steps ask what the default completion of partial data is, when abandoning it is forced, when the abandonment is correct, and how successive jumps compound. Specifically, we define a jump instance as a finite extension problem with a machine-checked certificate that a correct completion exists, is unique up to renaming, and differs from the canonical completion of the data. The canonical completion is given by the left and right Kan extensions and is also what models produce without constraints, so it serves as the default. We prove that jump instances are well-posed and establish a family theorem that certifies instances of unbounded difficulty without enumeration. We further formalize when a jump is correct and how successive jumps compound. Finally, we run the measurement on nine certified instances and four frontier models. The Kan-default rate is zero in all 248 constrained trials, so the models do jump at this step and abandon the excluded default every time. Failures at higher difficulty stem from exhausted reasoning budgets or constraint errors, never from reverting to the default. These results indicate that the second step is not the bottleneck. If the disputed incapacity is real, it lies in generating the constraints or inventing the framework. Code can be found at: https://github.com/EEthanShi/kan-jump-test.

items.title: Researchers find current knowledge-editing benchmarks fail to measure scope classification; INLAY gradient-free editor shows zero gain from per-query routing on 1,689 queries across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On Scope Classification and Current Knowledge-Editing Benchmarks: A Negative Result, with INLAY as a Gradient-Free Case Study
items.summary:
Researchers report that existing knowledge-editing benchmarks cannot effectively evaluate the scope decision of whether a stored edit applies to a given query. Using INLAY, a gradient-free editor designed to provide exact per-query ground truth, they tested every routing action on 1,689 queries spanning three datasets and input conditions, finding that no per-query routing method improved performance beyond a static policy.

The study identifies a structural issue in these benchmarks: they are counterfactual and lack negative examples, making it impossible to reward classifiers for abstaining or rejecting edits. By introducing a missing condition—excluding a query's own edit from the index for half the samples—the researchers observed measurable gains and abstention wins. They also note that INLAY was outperformed by other methods like WISE and retrieval-augmented generation on specific datasets, and disclose two minor bugs found during their audit that did not affect reported results.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every memory-based knowledge editor in the SERAC lineage depends on a scope decision: given a query, does a stored edit apply? We report that current knowledge-editing benchmarks cannot measure this decision at all. Using INLAY, a gradient-free editor we built to obtain exact per-query ground truth (the model is frozen, edits live in an external addressable memory, and applying an edit is a bias added along one token's unembedding direction at decode time), we execute every candidate router action on 1,689 queries spanning three datasets and three input conditions. An oracle router choosing the best action every time ties a one-line static policy to four decimal places in all nine dataset-by-condition cells: the maximum attainable gain of any per-query routing method is 0.00 points. Abstention is the sole winning action zero times out of 1,689. The cause is structural: these are counterfactual benchmarks whose evaluation question asks for the post-edit answer, so answering from parametric knowledge is wrong by construction, and a benchmark without negatives cannot reward a classifier's ability to reject. This generalizes beyond our system to the whole scope-classifier family the benchmarks are used to evaluate. We confirm the mechanism directly: constructing the missing condition ourselves, by withholding a query's own edit from the index for half the sample, moves pooled headroom from exactly +0.0000 to +0.0420 and gives abstention its first wins. We also report where INLAY itself does not win (WISE beats it on Qwen2.5-7B CounterFact, and retrieval-augmented generation beats every method we tested, INLAY included, on rigorously matched RippleEdits), and disclose two bugs found during a self-audit of our own routing machinery, neither of which changed a published headline number outside noise.

items.originalTitle: Co-Evolving Structured Knowledge and Reasoning in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers introduce KBevo, a co-evolving framework that simultaneously constructs a structured knowledge base and performs reasoning over it to enhance knowledge-intensive question answering. This approach optimizes both components end-to-end using question answering outcome rewards, allowing reasoning success to directly improve the knowledge base quality. Compared to standard retrieval methods over unstructured text, KBevo produces larger, better-connected knowledge structures with higher answer reachability and improved compositional factual reasoning and controllability. The framework addresses limitations of retrieval-augmented methods that often introduce irrelevant context and the brittleness and expense of traditional structured knowledge bases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented methods improve factual accuracy by grounding language models in external knowledge, but retrieving over unstructured text often introduces irrelevant context and offers limited control over the retrieved information. Structured knowledge bases offer a more controllable alternative, yet they are expensive to construct and often brittle to reason over. To address these limitations, we propose KBevo: a co-evolving framework that jointly learns to construct a structured knowledge base and reason over it for knowledge-intensive question answering. By optimizing both components end-to-end with QA outcome rewards, our method enables reasoning success to directly improve the quality of the constructed knowledge base. This leads to larger, better-connected knowledge structures with higher answer reachability, while also improving compositional factual reasoning and controllability compared to standard retrieval baselines.

items.summary: Researchers propose the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, a framework that builds dimensionality-optimized classifiers and develops diagnostics to identify which confident classifier decisions can be trusted, applied to prompt injection detection. The framework identifies influential prompts and tokens that affect classifier labels, categorizing prompts for safe reliance, heuristic flags, or human review. Applying this to a public prompt injection dataset, they find about 77% of confident decisions are sensitive to removing a single token, revealing two failure patterns: confidence calibration errors and exploitable shortcuts. The study also suggests remediation strategies for each diagnostic category and illustrates the framework through step-by-step examples.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a framework for constructing a classifier as a safeguard layer, and for developing a complementary diagnostic that identifies which of the classifier's confident decisions can be trusted. This framework, the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, consists of (i) constructing a dimensionality-optimized classifier, in which the embedding dimensionality is empirically selected via cross-validated performance rather than fixed a priori, (ii) locating a relatively small set of latent support vectors (~ 29% of total training examples) representing influential prompts for identifying tokens that alter the classifier's predicted labels, and (iii) utilizing such tokens and their associated attack magnitudes for constructing a diagnostic taxonomy. This diagnostic taxonomy provides an end-to-end guideline for flagging prompts that require different treatments: rely Safely on the classifier's decision; flag Heuristic Bias and Heuristic Override cases; route Insufficient Context cases for further human/safety review. Applying the framework to a classifier trained on a public prompt injection dataset, we find that a substantial fraction of its confident decisions (~ 77%) are not robust to removing a single token, and that this brittleness separates into two distinct failure patterns: a confidence calibration failure and a genuinely exploitable shortcut. For each zone of the taxonomy, we also recommend strategies for remediating diagnosed prompts. We illustrate the framework as a series of steps, demonstrating how each step operates.

items.title: Diff Mining framework identifies finetuning objectives by comparing logits of finetuned and base language models, enabling scalable detection of training fingerprints and biases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Diff Mining: Logit Differences Reveal Finetuning Objectives
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Diff Mining, a method that detects what a finetuned language model has learned by analyzing differences in output logits compared to its base model. This approach highlights salient tokens amplified during finetuning, serving as a fingerprint of the training even on unrelated text, and requires only access to output logits, making it scalable to large models.

The framework involves extracting per-context logit differences on a reference corpus and aggregating these signals into interpretable token sets using methods like Top-K frequency and Non-negative Matrix Factorization. Diff Mining outperforms existing model diffing techniques in finetune domain detection and identifies over one third of injected biases without targeted probing, suggesting its potential as an auditing tool for finetuning objectives.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finetuning has become the gold standard for refining existing behaviors and inducing new ones in language models, yet it often remains unclear exactly which behaviors emerge during this process. As models grow ever more capable, understanding finetuning better becomes increasingly important, particularly since unwanted behaviors may arise during finetuning. In this paper, we introduce Diff Mining, a simple yet effective framework for identifying what a finetuned model has learned by comparing its logits to those of its base model. Diff Mining effectively surfaces salient tokens that are amplified in the finetuned model, serving as a fingerprint of its training -- even on text unrelated to the finetuning domain. Unlike many existing model diffing methods which require model internals, Diff Mining only needs access to output logits and scales to large models. The framework consists of two modular stages: (i) extracting per-context logit differences between the finetuned and base models on a reference corpus, and (ii) aggregating the resulting signals to construct an interpretable token set representing the finetune. For aggregation, we explore both a simple Top-K frequency method and a Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)-based approach for disentangling multiple finetuning objectives into distinct token clusters. Empirically, Diff Mining succeeds across diverse settings: on finetune domain detection, it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art model diffing methods both in identifying relevant tokens and in downstream performance when an interpretability agent is given access to the extracted token set; on models with injected biases, it identifies more than one third of the biases without targeted probing. Overall, our framework shows promise in developing auditing tools to detect finetuning objectives.

items.title: Researchers propose J-Zero, a unified Challenger-Solver-Judge co-evolution framework for self-improving language models across verifiable and unverifiable domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: J-Zero: Unified Challenger--Solver--Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
items.summary: Researchers introduce J-Zero, a framework that enables language models to self-improve through adversarial co-evolution of a Challenger generating tasks, a Solver producing responses, and a Judge adapting preferences without external data. J-Zero outperforms baseline models by 4.2 points on verifiable tasks and 8.0 points on unverifiable tasks, maintaining improvement over at least ten iterations while baselines degrade after two. This approach addresses challenges in self-evolution for unverifiable domains by leveraging known preference orderings derived from response generation methods rather than relying on the Judge's own scoring.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving language models have recently emerged as a promising path toward superintelligence, with the advantage of reducing the cost of human supervision. While considerable progress has been made in verifiable domains, self-evolution in unverifiable domains remains substantially less explored. We propose Judge co-adaptation from Zero data (J-Zero), a unified Challenger--Solver--Judge co-evolution framework that supports self-improvement across both domains. The Challenger and Solver co-evolve through an adversarial interaction: the Challenger generates increasingly difficult tasks, while the Solver learns to produce higher-quality responses to them. In parallel, the Judge co-adapts using preference pairs whose ordering is known in advance from how each response was produced, i.e., the Solver's answer over the Challenger's, and its decomposed-and-recombined answer over its one-shot answer, rather than from the Judge's own scores. J-Zero outperforms the baselines by an average of 4.2 points on verifiable and 8.0 points on unverifiable domains, and continues to improve through at least ten iterations, whereas the baselines degrade after two.

items.title: Researchers propose FOCUS and RePAIR token-level guidance methods to reduce text degeneration in pruned large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FOCUS & RePAIR: Mitigating Text Degeneration via Token-Level Guidance for Pruned Large Language Models
items.summary: Pruning large language models (LLMs) can increase text degeneration, particularly repetition loops, despite stable perplexity and task accuracy. Researchers analyzed this issue at the token level, identifying loop entry risk and persistence as key factors, with persistence influenced by the escape mass of plausible token alternatives. They introduced two post-pruning fine-tuning methods: FOCUS, which reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher outputs to reduce leakage, and RePAIR, which uses positive and negative continuation pairs with margin loss to encourage plausible alternatives and prevent early repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended and instruction-based generation demonstrated that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve text quality.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pruning is a practical approach to compress large language models (LLMs), but it can amplify text degeneration, especially repetition loops, even when perplexity and task accuracy remain largely unchanged. In this work, we present a token-level analysis of this failure mode by viewing decoding as a dynamical process that enters and persists in a small set of recurrent contexts. Our analysis decomposes degeneration into loop entry risk and loop persistence, and shows that persistence is controlled by the escape mass assigned to plausible alternatives within the token sampling set. Motivated by these findings, we propose two token-level guidance objectives for post-pruning fine-tuning. FOCUS reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher regions to suppress leakage, while RePAIR uses onset-centered positive/negative continuation pairs with a margin loss to promote plausible alternatives and prevent early commitment to repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended continuation and instruction-based generation show that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve generation quality.

items.title: Researchers develop ContraTalk benchmark and Audio Twin framework to improve speech-grounded reasoning by addressing transcript-based shortcuts in spoken dialogue understanding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Text Misleads: Inconsistent-Aware Reasoning for Audio-Grounded Dialogue
items.summary:
Researchers identify a failure mode in spoken dialogue understanding where transcript-based shortcuts lead to incorrect interpretations despite conflicting acoustic cues. They introduce ContraTalk, a benchmark with 501 questions across five discourse dimensions, to evaluate models on both consistent and conflicting transcript and audio interpretations. The team also proposes an Audio Twin framework that converts speech into a text-readable representation of acoustic cues to enhance reasoning models' grounding in audio signals.

Experiments show that text-only large language models perform well on consistent cases but struggle with conflict cases, while direct audio models partially address this but still fall into transcript biases. The Audio Twin approach improves accuracy in conflict cases and reduces reliance on transcript traps, though its effectiveness varies with the underlying model architecture. These findings highlight the importance of integrating explicit acoustic evidence to diagnose and improve speech-grounded dialogue understanding systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.27176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding spoken dialogue requires joint reasoning over lexical content and paralinguistic acoustic signals such as emotion and conversational intent. However, existing evaluations often allow shortcuts based on transcripts or single-modality solutions, obscuring whether models genuinely ground predictions in speech. We formalize this failure mode as cross-modal disagreement, where transcripts suggest plausible but incorrect surface interpretations while acoustic cues such as prosody or speaking style support different answers. We develop a scalable framework that identifies text-biased surface interpretations and converts disagreement regions into conflict QA examples. We also include consistent cases where transcript-based and speech-grounded interpretations agree, enabling evaluation beyond adversarial audio dependence. This results in ContraTalk, a controlled benchmark containing 501 questions across five discourse dimensions: interaction behavior, emotion state, dialogue act, social stance, and conversational intent. We further develop an agentic-style reasoning framework that converts speech into an Audio Twin, a text-readable representation of localized acoustic cues that exposes acoustic evidence to the reasoning model. Experiments show that strong text-only LLMs exceed 90% accuracy in consistent cases but drop to 33-48% in conflict cases. Direct AudioLLMs provide only partial grounding, still selecting the transcript-biased trap in roughly 30-40% of conflict cases. Our Audio Twin framework improves conflict-case accuracy while reducing trap selection, but its consistent-case behavior remains backbone-dependent. These results identify transcript-based shortcuts as an important failure mode in spoken dialogue understanding and show that explicit acoustic evidence aggregation provides a more controllable interface for diagnosing and improving speech-grounded reasoning.

items.title: Researchers analyze how large language models represent moral knowledge using Moral Foundations Theory categories and geometric relationships in representation space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Language Models Organize and Structure Moral Knowledge
items.summary:
Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) organize moral knowledge by training linear probes on six Moral Foundations Theory categories and examining their geometric relationships in the models' representation space. They found that these moral dimensions neither collapse into a single detector nor isolate completely but instead span multiple independent dimensions with a shared moral-specific component, consistent across architectures and emerging early in pre-training.

The study also found no evidence supporting the individualizing/binding distinction predicted by Moral Foundations Theory, suggesting the models reflect corpus statistics instead. When applied to moral dilemmas, the models represented moral tension and conflict-specific structure rather than pre-resolved judgments, indicating that LLMs capture nuanced moral relationships beyond simple detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.27402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) organize moral knowledge? Models detect moral content broadly, but detection is a low bar. We ask whether they go further, distinguishing moral foundations from one another and organizing the relationships between them geometrically. We train six independent linear probes on open-weight language models, one per Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) category (care/harm, fair/cheat, lib/oppress, loy/betray, auth/subv, sanc/degrade), and examine how the resulting directions relate to each other in representation space. We find the directions neither collapse into a single moral detector nor isolate from one another. Rather, they span a near-maximal number of independent dimensions while sharing a positive common component. The shared component is the signature of integration, and it is moral-specific relative to a matched non-moral concept battery built identically (mean pairwise cosine 0.26 vs. 0.013). The geometry is consistent across architectures and scale and reaches its integration regime early in pre-training, well before probe accuracy saturates. The structure the model discovers shows no evidence of the individualizing/binding distinction predicted by Moral Foundations Theory (an underpowered test: only 20 candidate partitions exist) but rather reflects corpus statistics. Extending to moral dilemmas, each dilemma direction partially composes from its component foundations, at 2.7x a mismatched-pair baseline, while the majority of its variance encodes conflict-specific structure. The model represents moral tension itself, not a pre-resolved judgment.

items.title: Study analyzes rule- and model-based verifiers in mathematical reasoning, highlighting limitations in accuracy and robustness during reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Accuracy to Robustness: A Study of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers in Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary:
This study examines the reliability of rule-based and model-based verifiers used in reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning tasks. It finds that rule-based verifiers often fail to recognize equivalent answers in different formats, causing false negatives that hinder reinforcement learning performance as models improve. Model-based verifiers improve static accuracy but are vulnerable to reward hacking, misclassifying certain response patterns as correct, especially after fine-tuning.

The research provides a comprehensive analysis of verifier performance in both static evaluation and reinforcement learning scenarios, underscoring challenges in developing trustworthy reward systems. These findings offer insights for creating more accurate and robust verifiers to enhance reinforcement learning outcomes in complex reasoning domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.22203v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trustworthy verifiers are essential for the success of reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), which is the core methodology behind various large reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1. In complex domains like mathematical reasoning, rule-based verifiers have been widely adopted in previous works to train strong reasoning models. However, the reliability of these verifiers and their impact on the RL training process remain poorly understood. In this work, we take mathematical reasoning as a case study and conduct a comprehensive analysis of various verifiers in both static evaluation and RL training scenarios. We show that widely used rule-based verifiers fail to recognize equivalent answers in different formats, leading to substantial false negatives that increasingly hinder RL performance as the policy model gets stronger. Model-based verifiers substantially improve static accuracy but are highly susceptible to reward hacking during RL, where they misclassify certain patterns in responses as correct, particularly after fine-tuning. Our findings underscore the challenges inherent to both rule- and model-based verifiers and provide insights toward developing more accurate and robust reward systems for reinforcement learning.

items.title: AirLLM introduces a diffusion policy framework for adaptive LoRA fine-tuning of large language models over wireless channels, optimizing rank configurations to reduce transmission costs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AirLLM: Diffusion Policy-based Adaptive LoRA for Remote Fine-Tuning of LLM over the Air
items.summary:
AirLLM presents a hierarchical diffusion policy framework designed to improve remote fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on edge devices by adapting Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameters based on communication constraints. It uses a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent to generate coarse rank configuration decisions informed by wireless conditions and linguistic complexity, which are then refined by Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) to produce task- and channel-adaptive rank vectors. This approach addresses inefficiencies in fixed or heuristic LoRA rank settings and reduces over-the-air transmission costs while enhancing fine-tuning performance.

The system alternates optimization between the PPO and DDIM modules, with DDIM trained under a Classifier-Free Guidance paradigm to align with PPO rewards. Experiments across varying signal-to-noise ratios demonstrate that AirLLM consistently improves fine-tuning outcomes and communication efficiency, highlighting the potential of reinforcement learning combined with diffusion models for scalable and efficient remote LLM adaptation over wireless networks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.11515v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operating Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices is increasingly challenged by limited communication bandwidth and strained computational and memory costs. Thus, cloud-assisted remote fine-tuning becomes indispensable. Nevertheless, existing Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) approaches typically employ fixed or heuristic rank configurations, and the subsequent over-the-air transmission of all LoRA parameters could be rather inefficient. To address this limitation, we develop AirLLM, a hierarchical diffusion policy framework for communication-aware LoRA adaptation. Specifically, AirLLM models the rank configuration as a structured action vector that spans all LoRA-inserted projections. To solve the underlying high-dimensional sequential decision-making problem, a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent generates coarse-grained decisions by jointly observing wireless states and linguistic complexity, which are then refined via Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) to produce high-resolution, task- and channel-adaptive rank vectors. The two modules are optimized alternatively, with the DDIM trained under the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) paradigm to maintain alignment with PPO rewards. Experiments under varying signal-to-noise ratios demonstrate that AirLLM consistently enhances fine-tuning performance while significantly reducing transmission costs, highlighting the effectiveness of reinforcement-driven, diffusion-refined rank adaptation for scalable and efficient remote fine-tuning over the air.

items.title: Researchers propose Grounded Token Initialization to improve new vocabulary embedding in language models for generative recommendation tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Grounded Token Initialization for New Vocabulary in LMs for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: Researchers identify that the common practice of initializing new vocabulary tokens in language models as the mean of existing embeddings collapses distinctions among tokens, limiting fine-tuning effectiveness. They propose the Grounded Token Initialization (GTI) method, which grounds new tokens in semantically meaningful locations within the pretrained embedding space using paired linguistic supervision before fine-tuning. GTI outperforms mean initialization and other adaptation methods across multiple generative recommendation benchmarks, including industry-scale and public datasets, by preserving richer inter-token structure through fine-tuning, highlighting initialization quality as a key bottleneck in extending language model vocabularies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.02324v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models (LMs) are increasingly extended with new learnable vocabulary tokens for domain-specific tasks, such as Semantic-ID tokens in generative recommendation. The standard practice initializes these new tokens as the mean of existing vocabulary embeddings, then relies on supervised fine-tuning to learn their representations. We present a systematic analysis of this strategy: through spectral and geometric diagnostics, we show that mean initialization collapses all new tokens into a degenerate subspace, erasing inter-token distinctions that subsequent fine-tuning struggles to fully recover. These findings suggest that \emph{token initialization} is a key bottleneck when extending LMs with new vocabularies. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose the \emph{Grounded Token Initialization Hypothesis}: linguistically grounding novel tokens in the pretrained embedding space before fine-tuning better enables the model to leverage its general-purpose knowledge for novel-token domains. We operationalize this hypothesis as GTI (Grounded Token Initialization), a lightweight grounding stage that, prior to fine-tuning, maps new tokens to distinct, semantically meaningful locations in the pretrained embedding space using only paired linguistic supervision. Despite its simplicity, GTI outperforms both mean initialization and existing auxiliary-task adaptation methods in the majority of evaluation settings across multiple generative recommendation benchmarks, including industry-scale and public datasets. Further analyses show that grounded embeddings produce richer inter-token structure that persists through fine-tuning, corroborating the hypothesis that initialization quality is a key bottleneck in vocabulary extension.

items.title: Researchers present MOMO framework for robot skill adaptation using kinesthetic touch, natural language, and graphical interface, validated on a 7-DoF torque-controlled robot at Automatica 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MOMO: A framework for seamless physical, verbal, and graphical robot skill learning and adaptation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MOMO, an interactive framework that enables robot skill adaptation through three complementary modalities: kinesthetic touch for spatial corrections, natural language for semantic modifications, and a graphical web interface for visualizing and editing trajectories. The framework integrates components including energy-based human-intention detection, a tool-based large language model (LLM) architecture for safe natural language adaptation, Kernelized Movement Primitives for motion encoding, probabilistic Virtual Fixtures for guided demonstration, and ergodic control for surface finishing.

The tool-based LLM architecture generalizes skill adaptation from Kernelized Movement Primitives to ergodic control, enabling voice-commanded surface finishing. The approach was validated on a 7-degree-of-freedom torque-controlled robot demonstrated at the Automatica 2025 trade fair, showing its practical applicability in industrial settings requiring flexible and user-friendly robot adaptation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.20468v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Industrial robot applications require increasingly flexible systems that non-expert users can easily adapt for varying tasks and environments. However, different adaptations benefit from different interaction modalities. We present an interactive framework that enables robot skill adaptation through three complementary modalities: kinesthetic touch for precise spatial corrections, natural language for high-level semantic modifications, and a graphical web interface for visualizing geometric relations and trajectories, inspecting and adjusting parameters, and editing via-points by drag-and-drop. The framework integrates five components: energy-based human-intention detection, a tool-based LLM architecture (where the LLM selects and parameterizes predefined functions rather than generating code) for safe natural language adaptation, Kernelized Movement Primitives (KMPs) for motion encoding, probabilistic Virtual Fixtures for guided demonstration recording, and ergodic control for surface finishing. We demonstrate that this tool-based LLM architecture generalizes skill adaptation from KMPs to ergodic control, enabling voice-commanded surface finishing. Validation on a 7-DoF torque-controlled robot at the Automatica 2025 trade fair demonstrates the practical applicability of our approach in industrial settings.

items.title: Researchers propose HINT-SD, a targeted hindsight self-distillation method for training long-horizon LLM agents that improves efficiency and performance by focusing feedback on failure-relevant actions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HINT-SD: Targeted Hindsight Self-Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary:
Training long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents with reinforcement learning is difficult due to sparse outcome rewards that do not indicate which intermediate actions led to success or failure. Researchers propose HINT-SD, a self-distillation framework that uses full-trajectory hindsight to identify failure-relevant actions and applies feedback-conditioned distillation selectively to those action spans, rather than providing feedback at every turn.

Experiments on BFCL v3 and AppWorld benchmarks show that HINT-SD outperforms dense per-turn feedback methods by up to 13.60 percentage points on average while reducing training time per step by 2.26 times. This suggests that targeted feedback distillation is key to more effective and efficient training of long-horizon agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.17873v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training long-horizon LLM agents with reinforcement learning is challenging because sparse outcome rewards reveal whether a task succeeds, but not which intermediate actions caused the outcome or how they should be corrected. Recent methods alleviate this issue by generating rewards or textual hints from turn-level action-output signals, or by using feedback-conditioned self-distillation. However, generating feedback at every turn is inefficient when many intermediate turns are already successful or neutral, and applying feedback at a fixed or misaligned turn often fails to supervise the actions that contributed to the failure. To bridge this gap, we propose HINT-SD, a targeted self-distillation framework that uses full-trajectory hindsight to select failure-relevant actions and applies feedback-conditioned distillation only to targeted action spans. Experiments on BFCL v3 and AppWorld show that our method outperforms the dense per-turn feedback baseline by up to 13.60 percentage points on average while achieving a 2.26$\times$ reduction in time per training step, suggesting that selecting where to distill is key to effective and efficient long-horizon agent training.

items.title: Researchers propose TriShieldRAG, a three-layer defense framework to reduce poisoning attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems, cutting attack success from 79% to 1% on Natural Questions corpus [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TriShieldRAG: 3 Rings, One Blind Spot in Layered Defenses for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: TriShieldRAG combines document-level screening, trust-aware re-ranking, and cross-model consensus to protect Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems from poisoned documents that mislead large language models. While effective against non-adaptive attacks, adaptive attacks that alter document formatting can bypass the initial screening layer, resulting in high attack success rates similar to undefended systems. The study reveals that layered defenses relying on the same retrieved evidence can fail together, and cross-model agreement may be misleading in detecting attacks. The researchers have released the framework, evasion-certification methodology, and related artifacts for further study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.23838v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM answers in query-time retrieved documents, so reliability depends on what the retriever returns. PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., USENIX Security'25) showed five crafted documents mislead an undefended system in nearly 90% of cases, and that single-stage defenses give limited robustness. We propose TriShieldRAG, a three-layered framework: an Ingest Guard for document-level screening, a Retrieval Scorer for trust-aware re-ranking, and a Cross-LLM Consensus over three diverse models. We reasoned that collectively screening, re-ranking and validating retrieved evidence would give complementary protection, limiting the ability of poisoned documents to succeed through any single failure. We evaluate against non-adaptive and adaptive poisoning. Non-adaptively, on the full 2.68M-passage Natural Questions (NQ) corpus with the original PoisonedRAG attack, it cuts attack success from 79 +/- 1.0% to 1 +/- 0.0%. Adaptive attacks expose fundamental limits of layering. By changing only the document formatting, without modifying the poison text or accessing the retriever, the attacker reduces the Ingest Guard score from 0.500 to 0.000 and bypasses it on all 500 tested documents across three corpora. The remaining layers then give no protection: 62 +/- 0.8% attack success against a 56 +/- 2.5% undefended baseline on NQ, and 85 +/- 0.6% against 86 +/- 0.6% on HotpotQA. Layered defenses relying on the same retrieved evidence fail together: poisoned context misleads both re-ranking and consensus validation. Minority-poison thresholds prove corpus-dependent, at 0.214, 0.251 and 0.558 rather than the derived 0.5; a closed form we proposed for these failed a pre-registered prediction and is retracted. Cross-model agreement is misleading, reaching 0.96 while attack success approaches 99%. We release the framework, the evasion-certification methodology and artifacts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.13463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern image classification models excel when trained on single task-specific datasets but often struggle to generalize across domains and difficulty levels. We propose ARMDIL, an Adaptive Router for Multi-Domain Image Classification with LLMs. ARMDIL is an ensemble that uses a multimodal large language model (MLLM) agent to dynamically route each image to the most suitable vision backbone. Our diverse ensemble employs convolutional neural networks (ResNets), self-supervised representation learners (SSL), and vision language models (VLMs), each trained on a unified label space constructed from multiple image datasets with differing distributions and characteristics. Empirical evaluations illuminate the distinct capabilities and vulnerabilities of each architecture across disparate visual domains. Crucially, we show that ARMDIL effectively navigates these tradeoffs, performing competitively with specialized training-based routers. Furthermore, it drastically improves adaptability by allowing new information to be integrated via simple prompt modifications, while enhancing interpretability through natural language reasoning traces. These advances in cross-dataset image classification pave the way for more reliable general-purpose vision systems such as AI assistants and autonomous robots.

items.title: Survey catalogs 80 unsupervised post-training methods for foundation models, organizing them by internal update signals and analyzing their impact on model performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unsupervised Post-Training of Foundation Models: A Survey
items.summary:
This survey examines unsupervised post-training (UPT) techniques for foundation models, which adapt models using unlabeled inputs and learning signals derived from the models themselves rather than external labels or oracles. It catalogs 80 strict UPT methods, categorizing them based on the source of the update signal, such as prediction statistics, sample relations, self-generated targets, or internal evaluators, and explores how these choices affect whether post-training improves or degrades model quality.

The study introduces a framework combining input visibility and update persistence to map different deployment scenarios and guide the selection and evaluation of UPT methods. It highlights the importance of internal signal choice and task structure in determining the success or failure of unsupervised post-training approaches for foundation models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.24982v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation-model post-training usually relies on human labels, preference data, stronger teachers, or executable verifiers. We study Unsupervised Post-Training (UPT): update-bearing adaptation on unlabeled inputs whose learning signal is derived from same-lineage model artifacts rather than an external oracle. We catalog 80 strict UPT methods and organize them by the object that supplies the update signal: a prediction statistic, a sample relation, a self-generated target, or an internal evaluator. Beyond inventory, we show how the choice of internal signal and task structure determines whether post-training improves the model or recursively amplifies error. An orthogonal Input Visibility $\times$ Update Persistence view maps deployment regimes and defines a unified framework for UPT selection and evaluation.

items.title: DataKernelBench evaluates LLMs optimizing GPU-accelerated database queries, achieving up to 2.54× speedup on TPC-H benchmarks with H100 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
items.summary: DataKernelBench introduces a benchmark translating SQL into PyTorch TorchPlan programs to test large language models (LLMs) optimizing database queries on GPUs. It focuses on irregular, data-movement-heavy operators often overlooked by existing benchmarks and evaluates models on TPC-H workloads using CUDA and Triton on H100 GPUs. The strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieved a 2.11× speedup over the baseline, with kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes contributing to performance gains. The study also extended TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF to handle data exceeding GPU memory, achieving a 2.54× speedup on larger TPC-H datasets across four H100 GPUs. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to optimize complex database queries for GPU execution, emphasizing the importance of workload context over hardware context in performance improvements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.25061v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup. Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

items.title: Researchers find rank in QLoRA fine-tuning controls trade-off between factual acquisition and retention in Qwen3-4B model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning New Facts with QLoRA: An Acquisition-Retention Frontier
items.summary:
Researchers studied parameter-efficient fine-tuning using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) on the Qwen3-4B model to acquire new geographic facts while retaining unrelated capabilities. They compared full fine-tuning (FFT) with QLoRA at various ranks and found a clear acquisition-retention frontier: lower ranks preserved out-of-domain performance but acquired fewer facts, while higher ranks improved fact generalization at the cost of unrelated task performance. FFT retained general capabilities well but did not reach the highest factual acquisition levels.

The study used a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark and analyzed distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics, showing that higher-rank QLoRA moves the model farther from its pretrained state. A separate math adaptation experiment showed a weaker trade-off, suggesting the effect is more pronounced when learning new factual associations rather than reinforcing existing skills. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.25677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is often assumed to preserve pretrained capabilities because it updates only a small number of parameters. We show that this assumption depends strongly on adapter capacity. We study factual acquisition in a controlled OpenStreetMap-derived benchmark where Qwen3-4B must acquire anonymized geographic associations while retaining unrelated capabilities. Comparing full fine-tuning (FFT) with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) at ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64, we find that rank induces a clear acquisition--retention frontier. Low-rank QLoRA preserves out-of-domain (OOD) performance but acquires fewer facts, whereas higher ranks improve same-fact paraphrase generalization at an increasing cost in performance on unrelated benchmarks. FFT behaves as a conservative baseline: it retains general capabilities well, but does not reach the highest factual-acquisition regime. Distributional, weight-space, and spectral diagnostics mirror this behavioral trade-off, with higher-rank QLoRA moving farther from the pretrained model. A separate math adaptation experiment shows a weaker frontier, suggesting that the effect is most pronounced when adaptation must install new factual associations rather than reinforce skills already supported by pretraining. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zhngstl/new_facts_forgetting.

items.summary: Researchers have introduced CIFQA, a multi-agent framework that separates language understanding from numerical execution to enhance accuracy in financial question answering involving complex calculations. items.title: Researchers introduce Relational Hypergraph Transformer for multi-table learning with pentadimensional embeddings, improving semantic coherence on synthetic health records [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Methodological and Conceptual Framework for 5D Multi-Table Analysis: A Unified Approach for Complex Data Reuse
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a new architecture that models relational databases as hypergraphs and learns pentadimensional embeddings to address challenges in multi-table learning for complex data such as healthcare records. RHT uses sparse relational attention with reduced computational complexity and was evaluated on the synthetic Synthea electronic health record dataset for multi-label prediction of medical condition codes, showing improved embedding quality compared to existing methods.

The study found that while XGBoost achieved higher recall for rare medical codes, RHT produced more semantically coherent embeddings and maintained scalability. The researchers conducted ablation studies to assess the impact of architectural components and plan clinical validation on the MIMIC-IV dataset. The source code and experimental protocols have been made publicly available to support further research and application.

items.summary:

items.title: Study compares stratification and inverse probability weighting for correcting selection bias in retail inflation estimates, finding stratification generally more effective amid long-tail product distributions
items.originalTitle: Selection Bias Correction in Retail Intelligence
items.summary: A recent study investigates selection bias in retail intelligence, focusing on inflation estimation that often emphasizes popular products while neglecting niche items. The research uses simulations across four scenarios to compare Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) methods with stratification approaches for bias correction. Results show that stratification outperforms IPW in most cases, especially when data boundaries do not align with population breaks, maintaining low median errors. However, IPW with spline propensity models performs better under smooth polynomial relationships. The study highlights that violations of the Positivity Assumption limit the effectiveness of weighting methods in retail long-tail contexts, suggesting stratification as a more reliable correction method in such cases.

items.title: Study audits seven large language models on clinical pain speech transcripts, finding confident fabrication in some models despite lack of transcript pain cues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated seven large language models using the TAME Pain speech corpus, which includes transcripts of participants reading sentences while experiencing varying pain levels. The study found that while pain could be inferred from acoustic features, transcript-based predictions were near chance, indicating that pain scores derived solely from transcripts lack supporting evidence. Under cooperative prompting, most models abstained from predicting pain when transcripts contained no pain information and accurately identified pain ratings when present, but authority-framed prompts led to variable abstention rates and confident fabrication in two models.

The study involved 5,750 no-signal transcripts without lexical pain information and 1,294 transcripts with explicit pain statements. Six models abstained appropriately under cooperative prompts and achieved high accuracy in identifying spoken pain ratings. However, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B frequently produced confident but unsupported pain scores, with confident fabrication rates of 53% and 76%, respectively. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses.

These findings highlight challenges in large language models' robustness when handling uninformative clinical transcripts and underscore the importance of prompt framing in eliciting reliable model behavior. The results suggest caution in interpreting model outputs when underlying data lacks explicit signals.

items.title: GameWAM introduces a World Action Model for video games combining visual prediction and native control generation for closed-loop gameplay and GUI interaction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games
items.summary: GameWAM is a new World Action Model designed for video games that jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse actions, enabling closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. It handles heterogeneous native controls by predicting gameplay or GUI modes at each step and uses block-cycle control to plan actions over long horizons while preserving temporal continuity. Experiments show GameWAM achieves competitive task success with fewer native actions than comparable agents. The model also reveals a source-sensitivity failure mode called Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), where low-frequency action components influence coarse camera motion under fixed conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization. For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

items.title: Researchers analyze over-reasoning and under-reasoning in agentic AI, highlighting the need for adaptive reasoning allocation in evolving task demands [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI
items.summary: Recent research examines how agentic AI systems often misallocate reasoning efforts, leading to either excessive computation or incomplete solutions. The study evaluates these failure modes on benchmarks like MATH-500 and GAIA, finding that over-reasoning increases computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while under-reasoning results in incorrect or incomplete answers. The authors argue that future agentic AI should focus on dynamically adapting reasoning based on task requirements rather than fixed reasoning controls. These findings suggest a direction for developing more efficient and effective reasoning mechanisms in AI agents that interact with complex, evolving environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly adopted to complete complex, multi-tool workflows in real-world settings. However, existing benchmarks typically separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate agents in environments that are cleaner and more stable than those encountered in practice. We introduce DuMateBench, a real-session benchmark reconstructed from anonymized and privacy-screened user sessions collected from a large-scale production agent platform. Each task preserves the relevant pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, and is then validated through human verification. The resulting benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning 8 broad scenarios and 17 fine-grained capability categories, with most tasks requiring multiple capability coordination. We execute these tasks in isolated Docker containers injected with three forms of real-world environmental complexity: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy, and assess performance using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol. Experiments across five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial gaps in strict task completion. Complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses further show that performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by the capabilities of the LLM and the surrounding agent framework. The code and data are publicly available at https://dumatebench.com/.

items.title: SIGMA proposes a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework exploiting structured noise effects to improve robustness under noisy observations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SIGMA: Structured Noise-Effect-Aware Grouped Multi-Agent Aggregation
items.summary:
SIGMA introduces a hierarchical collaboration framework for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning that addresses structured noise effects arising from correlated observation disturbances among agents. It organizes agents into adaptive local groups for intra-group consensus and uses inter-group attention to maintain global coordination, enhancing robustness in noisy environments.

The framework was tested on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II, where it demonstrated consistent improvements in robustness while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free settings. SIGMA's approach explicitly models and exploits cooperation structures to smooth agent-specific deviations and integrate heterogeneous group contributions, addressing limitations of existing robust MARL methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces significant challenges in maintaining robust coordination under noisy observations. Although observation disturbances are often introduced independently across agents, their downstream effects on cooperative decision-making can become structured through underlying cooperation structures. We characterize this phenomenon as structured noise effects, where noise-induced decision effects exhibit local correlation among agents with stronger task-related dependencies while remaining globally heterogeneous across different agents and local structures. Existing robust MARL methods, however, rarely explicitly characterize or exploit such structure-dependent noise effects. To address this limitation, we propose SIGMA, a hierarchical collaboration framework that exploits cooperation structures to learn robust representations under noisy observations. SIGMA first organizes agents into adaptive local structures through density-based grouping and performs intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific representation deviations. Inter-group attention then adaptively integrates information across different groups to preserve global coordination while accommodating their heterogeneous contributions. Experiments on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II empirically validate the structured noise effects and demonstrate that SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.

items.title: Researchers propose Instruct-to-Act system combining vision-language model planners with world-model controllers for fast, language-instructable agent control across seven embodied environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Decoupling Planning and Control for Instructable Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Instruct-to-Act, a system that decouples high-level planning and low-latency control by training world-model controllers to act autonomously based on sparse, high-level text instructions from vision-language model (VLM) planners. This approach addresses the challenge of executing reliable action sequences in unfamiliar environments by combining VLMs' planning strengths with controllers' fast observation-to-action capabilities.

The team trains controllers using synthetic instruction relabeling and joint optimization of behavior cloning, reward maximization, and world modeling objectives. Evaluated across seven embodied and multi-agent environments, Instruct-to-Act outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation methods, maintains fast control, allows swapping of pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, and remains competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines on most tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that pre-trained, instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) perform well at mapping from instructions and observations to high-level plans, but struggle to realize such plans as reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control, but lack open-ended task guidance. In this work, we combine these strengths into a single system, Instruct-to-Act, where we train a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, higher-latency, and high-level text instructions generated by a VLM planner. To train controllers to be language-instructable, we relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. We evaluate our proposed approach across seven embodied environments, including three multi-agent environments where VLM planners coordinate through language while trained controllers serve as their actuators. Under matched observation and action spaces, our decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants, preserves fast control, and lets us swap in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose SymbolLKG, a Neuro-Symbolic architecture combining Logical Knowledge Graphs and dynamic solver routing to improve verifiable multi-step logical reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SymbolLKG: Towards Verifiable Logical Reasoning via Logical Knowledge Graph and Symbolic Solvers
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SymbolLKG, a Neuro-Symbolic framework that integrates an ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with a Logic Router to dynamically assign tasks to symbolic solvers, aiming to address limitations of Large Language Models in strict multi-step reasoning. The LKG models logical rules and constraints as topological nodes to explicitly capture dependencies extracted from text, supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism.

Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks show that SymbolLKG outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation baselines by delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths, offering a more rigorous verification mechanism for complex logical tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.26836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in natural language understanding, yet they struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, frequently suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing solutions like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) lack rigorous verification mechanisms, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often misses the complex, structural dependencies inherent in logical tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a Neuro-Symbolic architecture that integrates a Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with dynamic solver routing. Specifically, we introduce an ontology-based LKG that treats logical rules and constraints as first-class topological nodes, enabling explicit modeling of dependencies extracted from text. We further design a Logic Router to dynamically dispatch tasks to the optimal symbolic engine, which is supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism. Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.
